title: Compare the positions, not your first idea
outcomes: Compares the positions two candidate moves lead to, using a short checklist
Notices that a tie in material is where comparison starts
Recognises when there is nothing to compare
Writes down what decided a comparison

steps.text:
After you follow your candidate lines, compare **the positions they end in**, not the moves you like. Ask of each end position:
**1. Material? 2. Is a king exposed? 3. Is any piece loose or attacked by something cheaper? 4. Whose pieces are more active?**
The order is a suggestion. The first idea is only a candidate.

steps.caption: Black's bishop has taken on f3. White can retake with the pawn or with the queen. Compare the two end positions.

line.say: gxf3 retakes with the pawn. The engine rates this recapture best.
Black continues. The queen recapture would have been rated far worse.

claims.statement: gxf3 is the engine's best move.
Qxf3 is also a legal recapture.

steps.text:
**A tie in material is where comparing starts.** When two moves win the same material, look at the other three questions. And when the piece you like recaptures, picture the position first: the natural recapture is sometimes the worst one.
If a position has one legal move, there is nothing to compare.

steps.title: Same material, different positions
steps.prompt: Each position offers two ways to recapture. Predict which is better, then check.

steps.text: **What the app does for you now, and when it stops.** There is no checklist panel in this lesson; the checklist is the card above, and hints are offered on each item. A silent item switches hints and the engine off. The plan is to offer hints only on request once you solve items without them. Next item is silent.

steps.prompt: Look back at the silent item. Write down the two end positions you compared, in a few words each, and say which of the four questions decided it.

sources: docs/council-synthesis.md CD-3; Bilalic, McLeod and Gobet 2008 (a familiar idea can block a better one) [V, secondary]
